title: The principle of moments
prior_knowledge_summary: A couple contains equal, opposite, parallel forces with separate lines of action.
The torque of a couple is one force multiplied by the perpendicular separation of the force lines.
A moment is calculated from force and perpendicular distance from a chosen point to the force's line of action.
new_learning: State and apply the principle of moments for rotational equilibrium.
Separate clockwise and anticlockwise moments about one chosen point.
Choose a point that gives an unknown force zero moment.
not_yet_taught: the combined force and torque conditions for complete equilibrium
closed vector triangles for coplanar forces

visual_planning.reason: Six planned sketches support prediction, direction sorting, the controlled definition, pivot choice, two complete calculations and synthesis. No asset files are claimed in this text-only package.
visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

blocks.title: A heavy box can lose to a light box
content: A 300 N box sits 0.20 m from the pivot of a plank. A 100 N box sits on the other side. Where could the lighter box balance the heavier one?
The heavy box produces a moment of 300 x 0.20 = 60 N m. The lighter box can match it at 0.60 m because 100 x 0.60 is also 60 N m. Rotation depends on force and perpendicular distance together.

figure.purpose: Create a prediction conflict between force size and turning effect
figure.brief: Rectangular teacher sketch of a horizontal plank with a central pivot, a 300 N box 0.20 m to the left and an initially movable 100 N box on the right. Show curved direction arrows but do not reveal the 0.60 m balance position.
figure.alt_text: A heavier box close to a pivot and a lighter movable box on the opposite side of a plank.

blocks.title: Sort moments by direction
content: Choose one point first. For every force, imagine the turn it would produce about that point by itself. Put the moment in the clockwise or anticlockwise total.

Use the formula to remember M = Fd_perpendicular, written in the registry as M = Fd_⊥. Here M is moment in N m, F is force in N and d_⊥ is the perpendicular distance in m from the chosen point to the force's line of action.
Distance along an object is not automatically the moment arm. The shortest perpendicular distance to the line of action is the required distance.

figure.purpose: Teach clockwise classification and perpendicular moment arms
figure.brief: Teacher sketch with one chosen point, three force arrows on a beam, curved clockwise or anticlockwise arrows, and dotted perpendiculars from the point to each line of action. Keep labels sparse.
figure.alt_text: Forces on a beam are sorted by turning direction and linked to perpendicular distances.

blocks.title: Rotational balance
blocks.accepted_definition: for a body in rotational equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments about a point equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about the same point
content: The condition is about rotational equilibrium. The two totals must be taken about the same point.

A common shortcut says clockwise equals anticlockwise but misses both conditions. It feels sufficient because the equality is memorable. It fails when the moments were taken about different points or rotational equilibrium was never stated.
This lesson uses rotational balance only. It does not yet use a separate equation for the resultant force.

figure.brief: Split teacher sketch. Left panel shows clockwise and anticlockwise moment lists about point P with equal totals and a level beam. Right panel crosses out a comparison made about two different points. Include the label rotational balance.
figure.alt_text: Balanced moment totals use one common point, while totals from different points cannot be equated.

blocks.title: Balance three moments
content: A light horizontal bar is pivoted at P. A 24 N downward force acts 0.40 m left of P. On the right, a 10 N downward force acts 0.30 m from P and an unknown downward force X acts 0.55 m from P.
The 24 N force produces an anticlockwise moment. The two forces on the right produce clockwise moments. Rotational balance gives 24 x 0.40 = 10 x 0.30 + X x 0.55.
So 9.6 = 3.0 + 0.55X, giving X = 12 N. Check independently: the clockwise total is 3.0 + 12 x 0.55 = 9.6 N m, equal to the anticlockwise total.

figure.purpose: Model direction sorting, equation construction and an independent total check
figure.brief: Annotated worked layout with the bar, pivot P, all three forces and distances. Beside it show separate clockwise and anticlockwise columns, followed by a boxed equality check.
figure.alt_text: Three forces on a pivoted bar are organised into clockwise and anticlockwise moment totals.

blocks.title: Choose a point that removes an unknown
content: A force has zero moment about any point on its own line of action because d_⊥ = 0. This can remove an unknown force from the moment equation.

Imagine a beam joined to a wall at hinge H. The hinge force is unknown, but its line of action passes through H. Taking moments about H makes its moment zero. The remaining known forces can then determine a cable force or load position.
The unknown force has not disappeared physically. Only its turning effect about the chosen point is zero. A different point would usually give it a non-zero moment.

figure.purpose: Show why a point on an unknown force line removes that force from a moment equation
figure.brief: Two-stage hinge sketch. First show an unknown hinge force through H and label perpendicular distance zero. Second show the remaining load and support moments about H. Do not add a force-balance equation.
figure.alt_text: Taking moments about a hinge gives the hinge force zero moment because its line passes through the hinge.

blocks.title: Use a strategic point on a signboard
content: A uniform 3.6 m signboard is hinged to a wall at H. Its 420 N weight acts 1.8 m from H. A hanging lamp of weight 180 N acts 3.0 m from H. An upward support force T acts 3.6 m from H. The hinge force is unknown.
Take moments about H, so the unknown hinge force contributes zero. The support force is anticlockwise, while the two weights are clockwise: T x 3.6 = 420 x 1.8 + 180 x 3.0.

T = 1296/3.6 = 360 N. Check the units: N m divided by m gives N. Check the physics: the upward support acts farther from H than either weight, so a force smaller than their combined 600 N is reasonable.

figure.purpose: Teach pivot choice in a complete multi-force calculation
figure.brief: Hand-drawn signboard hinged at H with the stated distances, two downward weights, upward support T and a faint unknown hinge-force arrow. Add a calculation strip that crosses out the zero hinge moment and preserves N m units.
figure.alt_text: A hinged signboard calculation uses moments about the hinge to find an upward support force.

blocks.title: A reliable moments routine
content: Choose one point, preferably on the line of action of an unwanted unknown force. Mark every force and its perpendicular distance. Decide each turning direction. Add all clockwise moments and all anticlockwise moments, then equate the totals for rotational equilibrium.

Carry N m through the calculation and check the final size by substituting it back into both moment totals. A couple from the previous lesson can join one directional total directly because its torque is already a turning effect in N m.
The next lesson will add the separate force condition. Until then, do not claim that moment balance alone proves complete equilibrium.
